web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Engine — Index Sleeves, Swap Mechanics & Real-World Exposure
question: What economic exposure does a dollar invested in FAS actually buy, how does the 3x derivative sleeve reset at 4:00 PM ET, and what real-world financial businesses drive its 89 constituents?

epigraph.quote: An ETF ticker is a wrapper; inside it sits both a portfolio of operating businesses and a daily financing contract.
epigraph.author: Institutional Research Desk

web_blocks.title: Dual-Layer Architecture: Cash Equities + Total Return Swaps + Treasury Collateral

web_blocks.html: Unlike an operating company or a 1x passive ETF, FAS operates a two-layer financial engineering architecture managed by Rafferty Asset Management [1, 3]. On the asset side, FAS holds physical equity securities (or liquid sector proxies like XLF), U.S. Treasury bills, and institutional money-market funds as collateral [1, 10]. On the derivative side, Rafferty enters into over-the-counter (OTC) Total Return Swaps (TRS) with global investment-bank counterparties [3, 4].

To deliver 300% daily exposure to the Financials Select Sector Index, FAS does not borrow cash on margin. Instead, it holds roughly 80% to 100% of net assets in physical equities, XLF shares, and Treasury/cash collateral. It then layers 200% to 220% of notional exposure via total return swaps so combined daily sensitivity equals 3.00x NAV [1, 3, 4]. Under each swap, the counterparty bank pays FAS the daily total return of the Financials Select Sector Index. In return, FAS pays the counterparty a floating financing rate benchmarked to SOFR plus a negotiated spread [4]. Because swaps reset daily, FAS requires zero retail margin borrowing and carries non-recourse limited liability for shareholders [1, 2].

web_blocks.title: Underlying Benchmark Mix: 89 S&P 500 Financial Constituents Across Five Sub-Industries

web_blocks.html: Since August 1, 2022, every dollar of FAS's 300% daily exposure maps onto the Financials Select Sector Index. This benchmark is a float-adjusted market-capitalization slice of the S&P 500 comprising 89 holdings [5, 6, 10, 13]. To satisfy Regulated Investment Company (RIC) diversification rules, S&P Dow Jones Indices caps single-constituent weights quarterly [5]. Even so, the top ten holdings account for roughly 57% to 58% of index weight. Berkshire Hathaway Class B (~13.4%), JPMorgan Chase (~11.1%), Visa (~8.8%), and Mastercard (~6.5%) lead the basket [6]. On a $10,000 FAS stake ($30,000 gross daily exposure), you carry ~$4,020 of daily Berkshire sensitivity and ~$3,330 of JPMorgan sensitivity. You also carry ~$4,590 combined daily exposure to Visa and Mastercard [6].

web_blocks.takeaway: FAS is not a pure-play regional bank bet: roughly 55% of its underlying index weight sits in payments/multi-sector giants (Berkshire, Visa, Mastercard) and fee-heavy capital markets/asset managers, making it sensitive to both credit spreads and global payment/deal-flow volume.

web_blocks.title: Concrete End-to-End Example: How $10,000 in FAS Resets at 4:00 PM ET

web_blocks.html: To see this machinery in real dollars, consider a trader allocating $10,000 to FAS at the market open. At 9:30 AM ET, Rafferty's portfolio carries $30,000 of gross daily index exposure per $10,000 of NAV. That sleeve mixes roughly $9,000 in physical financial equities/XLF with $21,000 notional in OTC swaps, backed by Treasury collateral [1, 3]. Suppose the Financials Select Sector Index rises +2.0% that day. FAS gains +6.0% (before fee/financing accrual), raising the trader's equity to $10,600. Meanwhile, the underlying $30,000 exposure grew by 2.0% to $30,600—which is 2.887x the new $10,600 equity, not 3.00x. At 4:00 PM ET, Rafferty's execution desk must buy $1,200 of additional swap notional. That reset lifts tomorrow's opening exposure to $31,800 ($10,600 × 3) [3, 7].

Now trace the mirror image on a down day. If the index drops -2.0% from that $10,000 baseline, FAS falls -6.0% to $9,400. Gross exposure shrinks to $29,400, which equals 3.128x the new equity. At 4:00 PM ET, Rafferty must sell $1,200 of swap notional to cut exposure down to $28,200 ($9,400 × 3) [3, 7]. Thus, FAS systematically buys high after up-days and sells low after down-days. Consider a two-day whipsaw where the index rises +5.0% on Day 1 and falls -4.76% on Day 2 to 100.00. FAS rises +15.0% to $11,500 on Day 1, then drops -14.29% (-4.76% × 3) on Day 2. The fund ends at $9,857—a -1.43% mathematical decay despite a completely flat index [7, 8]. That path dependency is why holding duration and volatility regime dictate every outcome.

web_blocks.title: Real-World Sub-Sector Examples Inside Your $30,000 Notional Exposure
paragraphs: 1. Payment Toll-Booths (~15% combined Visa + Mastercard): Every time a consumer swipes a card at a grocery store or books an airline ticket, Visa and Mastercard collect basis-point assessment fees—high-margin, inflation-linked volume that cushions FAS against pure bank net-interest-margin compression [6].

2. Money-Center Banking (~21% JPM, BAC, WFC, C): JPMorgan Chase's 11.1% index weight means a $10,000 FAS position carries ~$3,340 of daily JPMorgan equity sensitivity—tied directly to commercial loan demand, deposit betas, and Basel III capital rules [6].

3. Capital Markets & Advisory (~25%): When Goldman Sachs closes a $10 billion M&A advisory mandate or BlackRock gathers $100 billion in ETF net inflows, fee revenue flows straight to operating leverage without balance-sheet credit risk [6].

book_paragraphs: When you buy a share of an operating company, you own a claim on factories, software code, or branch networks. When you and I buy a share of FAS, we are stepping inside a two-layer financial machine: an underlying basket of eighty-nine S&P 500 financial businesses on one side, and a daily-resetting derivatives contract on the other. Understanding both layers is non-negotiable if you want to know what actually moves your capital.

Let's peel back the wrapper first. Inside the Financials Select Sector Index, you might assume you are simply buying regional and money-center banks. In reality, banks account for roughly twenty-five to thirty percent of the index. Just as large is the Financial Services sleeve—anchored by Berkshire Hathaway at over thirteen percent and the global payment duopoly of Visa and Mastercard at roughly fifteen percent combined. Another quarter sits in Capital Markets firms like Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and BlackRock, with the balance spread across insurers and consumer lenders.

book_subsections.title: The 4:00 PM Reset: Tracing a $10,000 Position Dollar by Dollar
paragraphs: Now let's watch how Rafferty Asset Management turns that eighty-nine-stock index into three-times daily exposure. Suppose you put ten thousand dollars into FAS at the opening bell. To deliver thirty thousand dollars of daily sensitivity without borrowing cash in a margin account, the fund holds a core sleeve of physical financial equities and short-term Treasury collateral, then layers roughly twenty thousand dollars of notional exposure through over-the-counter total return swaps with major Wall Street banks.

Here is where the clock takes over. If the financial index rallies two percent today, your ten-thousand-dollar stake rises six percent to ten thousand six hundred dollars. Because the underlying thirty thousand of exposure only grew to thirty thousand six hundred, your effective leverage has drifted down below three-to-one. At four o'clock Eastern, Rafferty's trading desk must buy another twelve hundred dollars of swap exposure to bring you back to thirty-one thousand eight hundred. Conversely, if the index drops two percent, your stake falls to nine thousand four hundred, and the desk must sell twelve hundred dollars of exposure into the close.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: Think about what that 4:00 PM mechanical rule means in plain English: every single day, FAS is forced to buy more exposure after prices rise and sell exposure after prices fall. In a smooth, one-way uptrend, that compounding builds wealth faster than three times the index. In a choppy, sideways market, buying high and selling low every afternoon slowly grinds capital down.

book_subsections.title: Concrete Economic Drivers Across the Five Sleeves
paragraphs: That is why knowing the five sleeves inside the index matters so much for reading the regime. When you hold ten thousand dollars of FAS, you effectively hold roughly four thousand dollars of daily Berkshire Hathaway exposure, over three thousand three hundred dollars of JPMorgan Chase, and nearly forty-five hundred dollars combined of Visa and Mastercard. When consumer card spending is brisk and investment-banking pipelines are open, the payment networks and capital-markets firms act as a structural stabilizer. When credit spreads blow out and deposit flight hits regional lenders, all five sleeves correlate toward one, and the daily three-times multiplier amplifies every tremor.

Let's walk through a concrete example from each of the major sleeves so you can visualize the real-world cash flows behind the ticker. Start with the payment networks—Visa and Mastercard. Every time a family checks out at a supermarket or books a flight online, those networks collect a tiny basis-point toll on nominal dollar volume without taking a single dollar of consumer credit risk on their balance sheets. Next, look at JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America in the diversified bank sleeve: their earnings engine is the net interest spread between what they earn on commercial loans and Treasury securities versus what they pay depositors, supplemented by treasury-management and wealth fees.

Then look at Berkshire Hathaway, the single largest constituent at over thirteen percent of the index. Berkshire gives FAS embedded exposure to property-and-casualty insurance float, BNSF Railway, Berkshire Hathaway Energy, and massive short-term Treasury reserves—acting as an anchor of capital strength inside a sector often associated with balance-sheet leverage. Finally, the capital-markets sleeve—Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and BlackRock—translates IPOs, corporate debt issuance, institutional trading volatility, and global ETF inflows directly into fee revenue. Together, those eighty-nine companies form a diversified, cash-generative core; it is the three-times daily swap overlay that turns that core into a high-beta trading instrument.
